stories.title: A bigger mining fleet. Three dates to keep.
stories.dek: Luxxfolio’s update separates installed equipment, pool participation and an estimated treasury.
stories.status: Published November 12 · Treasury November 9 · Pool November 11
paragraphs: Luxxfolio reported that 50 additional L9 miners were commissioned, bringing its fleet to 338 machines and about 5.58 TH/s of nameplate capacity. Rated capacity is an equipment specification, not a guarantee of future production or revenue.

Its November 11 LuxxPool snapshot reported about 7.7 TH/s and 520 workers, including 2.1 TH/s from external miners. The estimated 26,838.23 LTC treasury and cumulative 3,599.13 LTC mined are dated November 9. Pool hashrate, fleet hashrate and treasury balances describe different things.

The company says 5% of LuxxPool’s own fees is allocated to the Litecoin Foundation; that is not 5% of miner rewards. Its wallet work involving MWEB and LitVM remains in development. The infrastructure story is useful precisely when delivered features and plans stay in separate columns.
stories.takeaway: Read the equipment specification, operating snapshot and financial estimate on their own dates.
stories.discussionPrompt: Which operating measurement would you want beside pool hashrate?

stories.title: Lightning’s quiet work: keep recovery paths intact.
stories.dek: LND’s pinned release notes focus on how nodes respond when transaction publication or reconnects fail.
paragraphs: The latest LND release observed in the official repository is 0.21.8-beta, published November 11. Its release notes describe correctness and recovery fixes rather than a new payment network or a promise of greater adoption.

The notes say transient or unknown sweep-acceptance failures retain inputs for retry. Funding-batch state is preserved after a publication error because the transaction may already have reached the network. The notes also describe channel reconnect and acknowledgement fixes.

A permanently unpublishable retained funding batch can still require manual cleanup after checking that its transaction cannot confirm. Reliable operation includes these limits. Operators should read the signed-release verification, backup and recovery instructions before changing software.
stories.takeaway: Recovery behavior matters alongside headline payment features.
stories.discussionPrompt: How do operators test that a failed publication can be recovered safely?

stories.title: A disclosed bug is not a newly discovered attack.
stories.dek: Three advisories explain historical risks and fixes; the affected version and configuration determine the story.
paragraphs: Bitcoin Core’s November 10 advisories describe previously fixed issues involving compact-block processing, Tor whitelist permissions and block-template creation during a reorganization. They are dated disclosures, not evidence of a new attack on November 18.

The Tor advisory concerns a non-default whitelist configuration: nodes without that setting were not affected. The compact-block and Tor issues are rated medium severity; the TRUC block-template issue is rated high severity. The published affected-version ranges and fixes should control operational decisions.

The official latest-release record points to Bitcoin Core 32.1, published October 28. Litecoin Core’s separate latest public release remains 0.21.5.8, dated September 12. These are checked software baselines, not new launches today. Use each project’s own verification instructions and release notes.
stories.takeaway: Keep disclosure dates, affected configurations and fixed versions together.
stories.discussionPrompt: What information should a useful security notice show before its headline?
